items.prompt: White to move. Do not judge yet, just look. Tap every square that the black knight on d4 attacks.
hints: A knight attacks by jumping: two squares one way and one square across.
Count from the knight: there are eight possible jumps and none leaves the board.
Two of the eight squares hold White pieces.
items.explain: A knight on d4 attacks eight squares: b3, b5, c2, c6, e2, e6, f3 and f5. Two of them hold White pieces, the pawn on c2 and the queen on f3. Counting like this needs no opinion, so it is an observation.

items.prompt: Tap the one White piece that is loose here: attacked by a Black piece and with no defender.
hints: Start with the pieces the black knight attacks.
For each of them, ask whether a White piece stands guard.
The queen has a guard. The pawn on c2 does not.
items.explain: The knight on d4 attacks the queen on f3 and the pawn on c2. A pawn on g2 defends the queen, but nothing defends the pawn on c2, so c2 is the only loose White piece.

items.prompt: Note: 'Bishop takes f7 with check wins a pawn for free.' This is a guess. Predict whether a test will confirm it. (Need an example first? The two boards just before this show how a test works.)
hints: After the bishop takes on f7 and gives check, what can Black do about it?
Count what White gives up and what White gains if the king takes the bishop.
A bishop counts 3 and a pawn counts 1.
items.explain: The bishop takes the pawn and gives check, but the black king simply takes the bishop. White gave a bishop (3 in counting values) for a pawn (1), so the guess fails. The engine agrees: this move is far worse than saving the queen.

items.prompt: Your queen is attacked by a knight. Find a move that saves it and also keeps the pawn on c2 guarded.
hints: The queen must leave the knight's reach, and you want a square from which it still guards c2.
Look at the first row, next to your king.
The queen goes back to d1.
items.explain: The knight attacks the queen, so the queen must move. On d1 it is out of the knight's reach and it guards the pawn on c2, so after the move nothing White owns is loose.

feedback_by_move.f3g3: The queen escapes, but c2 stays loose. The knight takes it with check and then attacks the rook on a1.
feedback_by_move.c4f7: The bishop takes a pawn with check, but the king takes the bishop. That gives up 3 for 1.

items.prompt: White to move. A note says: 'Castling worries me.' Which box does it belong in?
hints: Can anything on the board show how someone feels?
Castling is allowed here, and you can see that. The feeling is a different matter.
A feeling is about you, not about the position.
items.explain: Castling is legal here, and that is something the board shows. How nervous you feel is about you, not about the pieces, so no test on the board can settle it. It is still worth a line in your notes.

items.prompt: Black to move. A note says: 'Two white pieces attack the pawn on f7.' Which box does it belong in?
hints: Can you settle this by counting?
Follow the diagonal from the white bishop and the diagonal from the white queen.
The queen and the bishop both attack f7.
items.explain: The queen on h5 and the bishop on c4 both attack f7, and only the black king defends it. You can count that by looking, so it is an observation.

items.prompt: Black to move. White's queen and bishop both aim at f7. Find a move that deals with the danger.
hints: List what White threatens.
White threatens to take f7 with mate. You can chase the queen or add a defender.
One pawn move, one queen move.
items.explain: If Black does nothing, the queen takes f7 and it is checkmate. A pawn move to g6 attacks the queen, and the queen to e7 or f6 adds a defender. The natural-looking knight move to f6 allows mate at once.

feedback_by_move.g8f6: The knight attacks the queen, but the queen takes f7 with checkmate, because the bishop guards her.

items.prompt: Black to move. A note says: 'Black is in big trouble.' Which box does it belong in?
hints: Can you settle it by counting, or only by testing?
Test it: does Black have a good reply?
Black has several safe replies.
items.explain: It is a guess, and a test shows it is too gloomy. If Black replies with care, the engine rates the position as close to level. The danger is real but it only wins if Black answers carelessly.

items.prompt: White to move. A note says: 'The knight on c3 defends the pawn on e4.' Which box does it belong in?
hints: Can you point to it on the board?
A piece defends a square it could capture on if an enemy stood there.
A knight on c3 jumps to e4.
items.explain: A knight on c3 reaches e4, so it defends the pawn there. The queen on f3 defends it too, so the pawn has two defenders. Both are counts you can make by looking.

items.prompt: White to move. A note says: 'If the queen goes to d1, I lose my pawn on c2.' Which box does it belong in?
hints: Is this about what is on the board now, or about what happens next?
What would guard c2 once the queen stands on d1?
Test it: after the queen move, is anything loose?
items.explain: It is a forecast, so it is a guess, and the test says it is wrong. On d1 the queen guards the pawn on c2, and after that move nothing White owns is loose.

items.prompt: White to move. A note says: 'I have a bad feeling about this position.' Which box does it belong in?
hints: Can you point to it on the board?
Can a test or a count settle it?
It describes you, not the pieces.
items.explain: A bad feeling is about you, not about the pieces, so neither a count nor a test on the board can settle it. It is still worth one line in your notes.

items.prompt: Teach-back. A friend asks how an observation differs from a guess. Pick the best two-sentence explanation.

answer.class: An observation can be read off the board by looking or counting; a guess is a prediction or judgment that I label and test.
options: An observation can be read off the board by looking or counting; a guess is a prediction or judgment that I label and test.
An observation is a strong feeling about who is winning; a guess is a move I am sure about.
An observation is any opinion the engine shares; a guess is any opinion it does not.
They are the same thing; guesses are just observations I am less sure of.

hints: Which answer could a stranger check by looking at the board?
A guess is about the future or a judgment.
Look for the answer that says what you do with a guess.
items.explain: Looking and counting give the same answer to anyone who does them carefully, so they are observations. A prediction or judgment is a guess: say so, and test it if you can.
